issues.legal_issue: A second appellate court may not disturb a first appellate court’s finding of fact unless it frames a substantial question of law specifically addressing the legal defect relied on to challenge that finding.
material_facts: The trial court found the disputed property to be joint family property, but the first appellate court reversed that finding.

In the second appeal, the High Court framed the broad question whether the property was joint family property and stated that it could reappraise the evidence if the first appellate finding was perverse, unsupported, or based on misread evidence.
The High Court did not frame a specific substantial question of law concerning whether the first appellate finding was based on no evidence or was perverse, yet it reconsidered the evidence.
issues.conclusion: The broad question whether the property was joint family property was not, by itself, a substantial question of law. The High Court could not interfere with the first appellate court’s factual finding without framing a specific substantial question of law identifying the alleged defect.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a second appeal can be heard only on a substantial question of law, which must be framed. Under Section 96, the first appellate court is ordinarily the final court on facts. A factual finding may raise a substantial question of law if, for example, it is based on no evidence, material admissible evidence was ignored, inadmissible evidence was relied on, or the finding resulted from an erroneous application of law; the question addressing that defect must still be framed. The Court relied on Krishnan v. Backiam, Subramaniaswamy Temple, Ratnagiri v. V. Kanna Gounder, and Boodireddy Chandraiah v. Airgela Laxmi.

rule.if: second_appeal_proceeding and first_appellate_factual_finding and high_court_disturbed_finding and no_specific_substantial_question_framed

predicates.second_appeal_proceeding: The proceeding is a second appeal in which the High Court reviews a lower court decision.
predicates.first_appellate_factual_finding: The first appellate court made a finding of fact.
predicates.high_court_disturbed_finding: The High Court interfered with or reconsidered the first appellate court’s factual finding.
predicates.no_specific_substantial_question_framed: The High Court did not frame a specific substantial question of law identifying the alleged legal defect in the factual finding.

issues.definition: When a High Court in a second appeal disturbs a first appellate factual finding without framing a specific substantial question of law, it may not disturb that finding.

issues.legal_issue: A will’s provisions, read as a whole and in light of the surrounding circumstances, may vest a beneficiary with title to property acquired using funds set aside for that beneficiary even if the property was purchased in the testator’s name.
material_facts: The testator’s will set apart money for the benefit of his widowed daughter-in-law and grandson, including their maintenance and the grandson’s education and upbringing.
The testator contemplated purchasing immovable property for their benefit, and an immovable property was purchased soon after execution of the will using money set apart for them.

The property was purchased in the testator’s name, but after his death it was mutated in the daughter-in-law’s name and later in the grandson’s name; they alone possessed it, and other family members did not object to the mutation.

The will provided for supervision of the funds and their use for the beneficiaries, and the Court concluded from the will and surrounding circumstances that the testator intended to transfer the property’s benefit and title to them.
issues.conclusion: The title to the disputed property vested in the grandson, and the High Court’s contrary judgment could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 74, 82, and 84 of the Indian Succession Act require that testamentary intention be identified from the language of the will, read as a whole, giving effect to its provisions where possible and preferring a construction that gives a clause effect over one that makes it ineffective. The Court applied the principles in Navneet Lal v. Gokul, including the requirement to consider surrounding circumstances and place the court in the testator’s position, and relied also on Arunkumar v. Shriniwas, Bajrang Factory Ltd. v. University of Calcutta, Anil Kak v. Kumari Sharda Raje, and Shyamal Kanti Guha v. Meena Bose. The testator’s use of a particular term did not displace the intention apparent from the whole will and circumstances.

rule.if: will_interpretation_proceeding and testator_set_aside_funds_for_beneficiaries and testator_intended_property_for_beneficiaries and property_acquired_using_set_aside_funds and whole_will_and_circumstances_support_transfer

predicates.will_interpretation_proceeding: The proceeding requires the court to determine the effect of a will on property.
predicates.testator_set_aside_funds_for_beneficiari: The testator earmarked funds for the benefit of identified beneficiaries.
predicates.testator_intended_property_for_beneficia: The testator intended that property acquired with the earmarked funds benefit the beneficiaries.
predicates.property_acquired_using_set_aside_funds: The property was acquired using funds that the testator had set aside for the beneficiaries.
predicates.whole_will_and_circumstances_support_tra: The will read as a whole and the surrounding circumstances show an intention to transfer the property’s benefit and title to the beneficiaries.

issues.definition: When a will interpretation proceeding concerns property acquired with funds set aside for beneficiaries, and the will and circumstances show that the testator intended the property for them, the beneficiary takes title to the property.
